newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Weak NZ jobs data would add to easing pressure.
newsitem.headline: Weak NZ jobs data would add to easing pressure.

text.p: New Zealand jobs data due next week will paint a picture of a slowing economy and add pressure for monetary conditions to be eased, economists said on Friday.
"We're looking for weak data," said Bank of New Zealand treasury economist Peter Jolly.
"We're coming to the view of a proper (formal) easing," he added, refering to the prospect of a move by the central bank.
A survey of 10 economists predict Statistics New Zealand data due on Tuesday will see the unemployment rate rise to 6.2 percent from 5.9 percent in December.
More significantly, the jobs participation rate is picked to rise marginally to 65.78 from 65.5 and the employment growth rate to be 0.35 percent against -0.5 in December.
ASB Bank economist Anthony Byett, who expects the unemployment rate to rise to 6.2 percent, said overall the economy was worse than in the December quarter.
He also felt it would add to pressure for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) to ease but doubted it would ease yet.
"It is premature to come out with a (RBNZ) easing, but if we have another month of data in the same vein we've had in the last two or three weeks... I think they could afford to ease."
Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash gave a strong hint in a wire agency interview on Thursday that he was considering easing.

He said conditions were "still slightly stronger than we indicated as being desired on the 13th of March, and now... we're clearly in the process of looking at whether that line is still appropriate in preparing for our June Monetary Policy Statement".
Jolly said that comment appeared to reinforce views that current conditions were overly tight.
In March the bank indicated its desired monetary conditions were for a mix of the New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index at 68 and 90-day bank bill rates at 7.5 percent.
The TWI is now at 68.5 and 90-day bills at 6.83 percent, indicating conditions are slightly easier than desired in March.
Byett said the RB would be collating anecdotal evidence to back other retail and building data showing a slowdown.
Brash also confirmed that by commenting that he had noted recent surveys showing declining confidence.
"Another month down the track and it will be a convincing story that the economy is growing quite slowly, demand is falling and easier conditions are probably appropriate," Byett said.
But not everyone in the market is expecting weak jobs data.
Bankers Trust New Zealand is out of line with the consensus, predicting that the unemployment rate will fall to 5.7 percent and the quarterly employment growth rate will be 0.7 percent.
Economist Nick Bennenbroek said BT'S view was shaped by upward revisions to GDP data and the fact that employment is a lagging indicator. But BT's view of an easing is similar.
BT believes the jobs data will not be enough for the bank to ease and it must await confirmation from wages and labour figures later in May.

"At the moment I would say they would not assume a mix of monetary conditions that is tighter than in March and, if anything, they will assume something that is the same or slightly lower," said Bennenbroek.
"I see virtually no prospect of the Reserve Bank tightening and it is just a question of whether they go lower."
